marrow__BIOCHEM_CH06_Q001.takeaway: The TCA cycle occurs in the mitochondria.
marrow__BIOCHEM_CH06_Q001.displayText:
The tricarboxylic-acid cycle, also called the Krebs cycle or citric-acid cycle, occurs in the mitochondria. Its enzymes are located predominantly in the mitochondrial matrix, with succinate dehydrogenase as the important membrane-bound exception.

The cycle operates in aerobic tissues and oxidizes acetyl-CoA while generating reduced cofactors for oxidative phosphorylation.

rationales.a: The cytosol is not the site of the TCA cycle.
rationales.b: The endoplasmic reticulum does not house the TCA-cycle enzyme system.
rationales.d: Lysosomes are involved in intracellular degradation rather than the TCA cycle.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH06_Q002.takeaway: The Krebs cycle is the final common oxidative pathway for carbohydrate, lipid and protein metabolism.
marrow__BIOCHEM_CH06_Q002.displayText:
The Krebs cycle is the final common pathway for oxidation of carbohydrates, lipids and proteins because these fuels converge on acetyl-CoA or TCA-cycle intermediates.

Acetyl-CoA—not pyruvate—condenses with oxaloacetate to form citrate. Oxidative phosphorylation occurs in mitochondria, and α-ketoglutarate is a five-carbon compound.

rationales.b: Pyruvate is first converted to acetyl-CoA; acetyl-CoA is the molecule that condenses with oxaloacetate to form citrate.
rationales.c: Oxidative phosphorylation occurs on the inner mitochondrial membrane, not in the cytoplasm.
rationales.d: α-Ketoglutarate contains five carbons, not four.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH06_Q003.takeaway: Acetyl-CoA enters the TCA cycle but is not itself a cycle intermediate.
marrow__BIOCHEM_CH06_Q003.displayText:
Acetyl-CoA is a starting substrate for the TCA cycle rather than an intermediate regenerated within the cycle. It condenses with oxaloacetate to form citrate.

Citrate, succinyl-CoA and fumarate are genuine TCA-cycle intermediates. Acetyl-CoA can be supplied by carbohydrate metabolism, fatty-acid oxidation and ketogenic amino-acid metabolism. The source pathway figure remains preserved separately.

rationales.a: Citrate is formed within the TCA cycle and is a cycle intermediate.
rationales.c: Succinyl-CoA is a TCA-cycle intermediate formed from α-ketoglutarate.
rationales.d: Fumarate is a TCA-cycle intermediate formed from succinate.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH06_Q004.takeaway: Hyperammonemia depletes α-ketoglutarate and thereby suppresses the TCA cycle.
marrow__BIOCHEM_CH06_Q004.displayText:
In hyperammonemia, excess ammonia is incorporated into glutamate to form glutamine. As glutamate is consumed, α-ketoglutarate is diverted from the TCA cycle to regenerate glutamate.

This progressive depletion of α-ketoglutarate removes an important TCA-cycle intermediate and can impair energy production.

rationales.a: Oxaloacetate is not the source-keyed intermediate primarily depleted by ammonia trapping in this mechanism.
rationales.c: Succinyl-CoA is not the TCA intermediate specifically depleted by hyperammonemia in the source explanation.
rationales.d: Fumarate is not the source-keyed metabolite depleted through glutamate/glutamine formation.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH06_Q005.takeaway: Aconitase is an iron-containing enzyme that converts citrate to isocitrate.
marrow__BIOCHEM_CH06_Q005.displayText:
Aconitase contains iron and catalyzes the reversible conversion of citrate to isocitrate. The reaction proceeds through cis-aconitate: citrate is first dehydrated and then rehydrated to form isocitrate.

The source also notes aconitase's relationship to iron homeostasis. Its reaction diagram remains preserved separately.

rationales.a: Calcium is not the metal component identified for aconitase.
rationales.b: Magnesium is not the source-keyed metal contained in aconitase.
rationales.d: Manganese is not the characteristic metal component of aconitase.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH06_Q006.takeaway: Fluoroacetate inhibits aconitase after conversion to fluorocitrate.
marrow__BIOCHEM_CH06_Q006.displayText:
Fluoroacetate is metabolically activated to fluoroacetyl-CoA, which condenses with oxaloacetate to form fluorocitrate. Fluorocitrate then inhibits aconitase.

This blocks the citrate-to-isocitrate step of the TCA cycle.

rationales.a: Arsenite inhibits α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase rather than aconitase.
rationales.d: Iodoacetate inhibits glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase in glycolysis, not aconitase.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH06_Q007.takeaway: Valine enters the TCA cycle at the succinyl-CoA level.
marrow__BIOCHEM_CH06_Q007.displayText:
Valine is a glucogenic amino acid whose carbon skeleton is ultimately converted through propionyl-CoA and methylmalonyl-CoA to succinyl-CoA.

It therefore enters the TCA cycle at succinyl-CoA. The source amino-acid entry-point table remains preserved separately.

rationales.a: α-Ketoglutarate is the entry point for amino acids such as glutamate, not valine.
rationales.b: Fumarate is an entry point for other amino-acid carbon skeletons but not the source-keyed entry for valine.
rationales.d: Acetyl-CoA is not the TCA entry point of valine.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH06_Q008.takeaway: The first CO₂ of the TCA cycle is released by isocitrate dehydrogenase.
marrow__BIOCHEM_CH06_Q008.displayText:
Isocitrate dehydrogenase catalyzes the first oxidative decarboxylation of the TCA cycle: isocitrate is converted to α-ketoglutarate while CO₂ is released and NAD⁺ is reduced to NADH.

The second oxidative decarboxylation occurs when α-ketoglutarate is converted to succinyl-CoA by α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase. The source Krebs-cycle figure remains preserved separately.

rationales.a: Aconitase converts citrate to isocitrate without releasing CO₂.
rationales.c: Succinate thiokinase converts succinyl-CoA to succinate and generates GTP; it does not catalyze the first decarboxylation.
rationales.d: Succinate dehydrogenase converts succinate to fumarate without releasing CO₂.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH06_Q009.takeaway: Isocitrate dehydrogenase requires Mg²⁺ or Mn²⁺; Mn²⁺ is the listed correct cofactor.
marrow__BIOCHEM_CH06_Q009.displayText:
Isocitrate dehydrogenase catalyzes oxidative decarboxylation of isocitrate to α-ketoglutarate. The reaction requires a divalent metal ion, classically Mg²⁺ or Mn²⁺.

Among the listed options, Mn²⁺ is therefore correct.

rationales.a: Copper is not the divalent metal cofactor specified for isocitrate dehydrogenase.
rationales.c: Iron is not the source-keyed metal cofactor for this reaction.
rationales.d: Calcium is not the required catalytic metal listed for isocitrate dehydrogenase.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH06_Q010.takeaway: The only substrate-level phosphorylation in the TCA cycle occurs at succinyl-CoA → succinate.
marrow__BIOCHEM_CH06_Q010.displayText:
Succinyl-CoA is converted to succinate by succinyl-CoA synthetase, also called succinate thiokinase. This reaction generates GTP directly and is the only substrate-level phosphorylation step of the TCA cycle.

The source pathway figure remains preserved separately.

rationales.a: Isocitrate → α-ketoglutarate generates NADH and CO₂, not GTP by substrate-level phosphorylation.
rationales.b: α-Ketoglutarate → succinyl-CoA produces NADH and CO₂ but is not the substrate-level phosphorylation step.
rationales.d: Succinate → fumarate generates FADH₂ through succinate dehydrogenase rather than directly producing GTP.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH06_Q011.takeaway: One turn of the TCA cycle yields about 10 ATP equivalents.
marrow__BIOCHEM_CH06_Q011.displayText:
Per acetyl-CoA oxidized, one turn of the TCA cycle produces 3 NADH, 1 FADH₂ and 1 GTP.

Using the source ATP equivalents: 3 NADH = 7.5 ATP, 1 FADH₂ = 1.5 ATP and 1 GTP = 1 ATP. Total yield = 10 ATP equivalents per turn.

rationales.b: 20 ATP is double the source-calculated yield for one turn of the cycle.
rationales.c: 25 ATP exceeds the energy captured from 3 NADH, 1 FADH₂ and 1 GTP.
rationales.d: 30 ATP is far above the source-keyed yield from a single acetyl-CoA turn.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH06_Q012.takeaway: Biotin is not a cofactor used by the TCA-cycle enzymes listed in the source.
marrow__BIOCHEM_CH06_Q012.displayText:
Biotin is the exception. The TCA cycle uses vitamin-derived cofactors including riboflavin-derived FAD, niacin-derived NAD⁺, thiamine pyrophosphate and coenzyme A derived from pantothenic acid.

Biotin is primarily a cofactor for carboxylation reactions and is not one of the TCA-cycle cofactors in this comparison.

rationales.b: Pantothenic acid contributes to coenzyme A, which participates in acetyl-CoA and succinyl-CoA metabolism.
rationales.c: Riboflavin supplies FAD, the cofactor used by succinate dehydrogenase.
rationales.d: Niacin supplies NAD⁺, used by several TCA-cycle dehydrogenases.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH06_Q013.takeaway: The TCA cycle is amphibolic because it participates in both catabolic oxidation and anabolic synthesis.
marrow__BIOCHEM_CH06_Q013.displayText:
The TCA cycle is called amphibolic because it serves both oxidative and synthetic roles. It oxidizes acetyl-CoA to capture energy, while its intermediates also supply carbon skeletons for biosynthetic pathways.

TCA intermediates contribute to processes such as amino-acid synthesis, gluconeogenesis and fatty-acid synthesis.

rationales.b: Use of TCA metabolites in other pathways is part of its anabolic role, but the defining concept of amphibolic is the combination of catabolic and anabolic functions.
rationales.c: The TCA cycle is not called amphibolic because the entire cycle simply runs forward and backward.
rationales.d: The term does not refer to using the same enzymes in reverse direction.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH06_Q014.displayText:
Arsenite inhibits the α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase complex. This enzyme carries out oxidative decarboxylation of α-ketoglutarate to succinyl-CoA.

The source inhibitor table contrasts aconitase–fluoroacetate, α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase–arsenite and succinate dehydrogenase–malonate; the native table remains preserved separately.

rationales.a: Iodoacetate is a glycolytic inhibitor and is not the source-keyed inhibitor of α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH06_Q015.takeaway: Pyridoxal phosphate is not one of the five cofactors of α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase.
marrow__BIOCHEM_CH06_Q015.displayText:
The α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase complex uses five classic cofactors: thiamine pyrophosphate, lipoate, coenzyme A, FAD and NAD⁺.

Pyridoxal phosphate is therefore the exception. The same five-cofactor pattern is shared by other oxidative-decarboxylation complexes such as pyruvate dehydrogenase and branched-chain α-ketoacid dehydrogenase.

rationales.a: Lipoate is one of the required cofactors of α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase.
rationales.b: Thiamine pyrophosphate is required for oxidative decarboxylation in the complex.
rationales.c: FAD is one of the five cofactors used by the complex.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH06_Q016.takeaway: Pyruvate kinase is not a component of the pyruvate-dehydrogenase complex.
marrow__BIOCHEM_CH06_Q016.displayText:
The pyruvate dehydrogenase complex contains three enzyme components: pyruvate dehydrogenase, dihydrolipoyl transacetylase and dihydrolipoyl dehydrogenase.

Pyruvate kinase is a glycolytic enzyme that catalyzes phosphoenolpyruvate → pyruvate with ATP generation; it is not part of the PDH complex. PDH converts pyruvate to acetyl-CoA by oxidative decarboxylation.

rationales.a: Pyruvate dehydrogenase is the E1 enzyme component of the PDH complex.
rationales.b: Dihydrolipoyl transacetylase is the E2 component of the PDH complex.
rationales.d: Dihydrolipoyl dehydrogenase is the E3 component of the PDH complex.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH06_Q017.takeaway: Thiamine deficiency inhibits pyruvate dehydrogenase, reducing conversion of pyruvate to acetyl-CoA.
marrow__BIOCHEM_CH06_Q017.displayText:
Thiamine pyrophosphate is a required cofactor for pyruvate dehydrogenase. In thiamine deficiency, the PDH reaction is impaired, so conversion of pyruvate to acetyl-CoA is reduced.

Pyruvate may then accumulate and be diverted toward lactate, contributing to lactic acidosis. The source pathway figure remains preserved separately.

rationales.a: Isocitrate → α-ketoglutarate is catalyzed by isocitrate dehydrogenase and does not depend on thiamine.
rationales.b: Succinate → fumarate is catalyzed by FAD-dependent succinate dehydrogenase.
rationales.d: Fumarate → malate is catalyzed by fumarase and does not require thiamine.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH06_Q018.takeaway: Acetyl-CoA is an allosteric inhibitor of the pyruvate-dehydrogenase complex.
marrow__BIOCHEM_CH06_Q018.displayText:
High-energy and product signals suppress pyruvate dehydrogenase. The source lists NADH, acetyl-CoA and ATP as allosteric inhibitors of the PDH complex.

Acetyl-CoA therefore provides product feedback that limits further conversion of pyruvate to acetyl-CoA when mitochondrial energy supply is already abundant.

rationales.a: AMP signals low energy and is not a source-keyed allosteric inhibitor of PDH.
rationales.b: ADP is associated with low-energy signaling rather than inhibition of PDH in this comparison.
rationales.d: Citrate is not one of the PDH allosteric inhibitors listed by the source.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH06_Q019.takeaway: Inherited pyruvate-dehydrogenase deficiency can cause congenital lactic acidosis.
marrow__BIOCHEM_CH06_Q019.displayText:
Deficiency of one or more components of the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex prevents efficient conversion of pyruvate to acetyl-CoA. Pyruvate is then diverted toward lactate, producing lactic acidosis.

The source includes PDH deficiency among important causes of lactic acidosis together with tissue hypoxia, mitochondrial disease, TCA-cycle enzyme defects, thiamine deficiency and selected poisons.

rationales.b: Pyruvate-kinase deficiency primarily causes hemolytic anemia rather than the congenital lactic-acidosis pattern asked here.
rationales.c: Pyruvate decarboxylase is not the human mitochondrial enzyme complex responsible for conversion of pyruvate to acetyl-CoA.
rationales.d: Transketolase impairment can reflect thiamine deficiency but is not the source-keyed enzyme defect causing congenital lactic acidosis.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH06_Q020.takeaway: Pyruvate → oxaloacetate is an anaplerotic reaction that replenishes the TCA cycle.
marrow__BIOCHEM_CH06_Q020.displayText:
Pyruvate carboxylase converts pyruvate to oxaloacetate. This is an anaplerotic reaction because it replenishes a TCA-cycle intermediate that may have been withdrawn for biosynthesis.

Acetyl-CoA activates pyruvate carboxylase, helping maintain enough oxaloacetate for condensation with acetyl-CoA and continued TCA-cycle function.

rationales.a: Pyruvate → acetyl-CoA supplies the entering acetyl group but does not replenish a TCA-cycle intermediate.
rationales.c: Conversion of pyruvate to acetaldehyde is not a human anaplerotic TCA reaction.
rationales.d: Pyruvate → lactate regenerates NAD⁺ during anaerobic glycolysis and does not replenish the TCA-cycle intermediate pool.
